families.name: Spectral Hypergraph Convolution
families.definition: Methods that perform convolution on hypergraphs by leveraging spectral properties, such as hypergraph Laplacians or Markov chains, to capture high-order relationships.

properties.text: These methods utilize algebraic descriptors like the hypergraph Laplacian or magnetic Laplacian to define convolution operations.
They can model non-reversible Markov chains to preserve directional or asymmetric information in hyperedges.
Spectral approaches allow for the derivation of random walk-based Laplacians and mixing time bounds for hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights.
They provide a theoretical foundation for understanding how hypergraph structures influence node embeddings through energy minimization.

limitations.text: Many spectral methods reduce hypergraphs to undirected graphs via symmetrized matrix representations, potentially losing important directional or higher-order information.
The computational complexity of high-dimensional hypergraph descriptors, such as tensors, can be prohibitive.
Spectral methods often rely on pre-defined or static hypergraph topologies, limiting their ability to adapt to dynamic or noisy structures.

families.name: Spatial Hypergraph Message Passing
families.definition: Architectures that propagate information between nodes and hyperedges through explicit message-passing mechanisms, often following a node-to-hyperedge-to-node paradigm.

properties.text: These methods typically adopt a two-stage message passing paradigm where information flows from nodes to hyperedges and back to nodes.
They can be extended to handle directed hypergraphs by defining specific propagation rules for source and destination node sets.
Spatial approaches allow for the integration of attention mechanisms to weigh the importance of different hyperedges or nodes.
They support the modeling of edge-dependent node features, allowing nodes to have different representations in different hyperedges.

limitations.text: The standard two-stage paradigm often focuses on local information propagation and may fail to capture global structural information effectively.
Heuristic propagation rules in many existing methods lead to suboptimal performance on certain datasets.
Message passing on hypergraphs can suffer from over-smoothing, where node representations become indistinguishable in deep networks.

families.name: Hypergraph Structure Learning
families.definition: Techniques that dynamically infer or optimize the hypergraph structure (nodes and hyperedges) during the learning process rather than relying on a fixed input structure.

properties.text: These methods adaptively optimize hypergraph structures to capture hidden correlations and reduce dependence on noisy or incomplete initial structures.
They can adjust the number of hyperedges to better fit the underlying data distribution.
Structure learning enables the discovery of task-specific latent relationships that are not explicitly present in the raw data.
Dynamic construction modules can be stacked with convolution layers to iteratively refine the hypergraph representation.

limitations.text: The space of possible hypergraph structures grows super-exponentially with the number of nodes, making optimization challenging.
Most existing dynamic methods cannot fully explore the underlying structure if they are constrained to a fixed number of hyperedges.
Learning both the structure and the model parameters simultaneously can be unstable without sufficient supervision or self-supervision signals.

families.name: Self-Supervised and Contrastive Hypergraph Learning
families.definition: Unsupervised representation learning methods that use pretext tasks, such as contrastive learning or autoencoding, to learn node and hyperedge embeddings without labels.

properties.text: These methods maximize agreements among node embeddings or group-wise collective behaviors within hypergraphs.
They employ augmentation strategies, such as masking or sampling, to create positive and negative pairs for contrastive optimization.
Self-supervised approaches can leverage virtual label propagation or mutual information maximization to handle featureless or label-free hypergraphs.
They aim to capture high-order relationships in unlabeled data by distinguishing similar and dissimilar hypergraph structures.

limitations.text: Arbitrary selection of negative samples in contrastive methods can be unreliable and cause training bias.
Many methods require a large number of negative samples, leading to high computational costs.
Existing self-supervised models often neglect the capture of group-wise collective behaviors, focusing instead on individual node embeddings.

families.name: Hypergraph Expansion and Transformation
families.definition: Approaches that transform hypergraphs into standard graphs or other structures (e.g., line graphs, clique expansions) to enable the use of existing graph neural network algorithms.

properties.text: These methods convert hypergraphs into standard graphs while attempting to preserve high-order information.
Line expansion treats vertices and hyperedges equally by modeling vertex-hyperedge pairs, inducing a homogeneous structure.
Cross expansion methods transform both hypervertices and hyperedges into a joint representation space.
They allow for the direct application of well-established graph learning algorithms to hypergraph data.

limitations.text: Transformation methods like clique or star expansion can lead to information loss or redundancy.
Expansions may not fully capture the symmetric nature of data co-occurrence if they focus solely on vertex or hyperedge levels.
The resulting standard graphs may be much larger than the original hypergraphs, increasing computational complexity.

families.name: Higher-Order Network Analysis and Theory
families.definition: Theoretical and analytical studies that examine the structural properties, dynamics, and expressiveness of hypergraphs and higher-order networks.

properties.text: These works define and measure structural properties such as transitivity, reciprocity, and hyperedge overlap in real-world hypergraphs.
They analyze the expressiveness of hypergraph neural networks, establishing hierarchies of problems solvable based on depth and edge arity.
Theoretical frameworks investigate how higher-order interactions shape collective behaviors in complex systems, such as social contagion or microbial communities.
They provide insights into the limitations of pairwise graph models and the necessity of higher-order structures for accurate modeling.

limitations.text: There is a lack of systematic measures for certain properties, such as reciprocity in general directed hypergraphs.
Theoretical analyses often assume idealized conditions that may not hold in noisy, real-world data.
Understanding the generalization of hypergraph neural networks to arbitrary input sizes remains an open theoretical challenge.
How to effectively model edge-dependent node features where a node's label or representation varies across different hyperedges.
How to handle the extreme class imbalance in hyperlink prediction, where the number of non-hyperedges grows exponentially with the number of nodes.
How to balance the trade-off between the complexity of higher-order interactions and the accuracy of downstream tasks, determining how much abstraction is sufficient.
How to develop efficient negative sampling strategies for hyperedge prediction that are both reliable and computationally feasible.
How to extend graph neural network architectures to fully relational structures, such as k-ary relations in relational hypergraphs, for link prediction.
How to capture global information in hypergraph message passing, as current two-stage paradigms are limited to local propagation.
How to design hypergraph neural networks that are robust to heterophily, where adjacent nodes or hyperedges exhibit dissimilar labels or features.
How to integrate topological features and structural insights into hypergraph transformers to improve representation learning beyond semantic feature-based attention.
How to model the temporal dynamics of high-order interactions in sequential or longitudinal data, such as clinical pathways or stock movements.
How to unify the design paradigms of graph and hypergraph neural networks to create universal frameworks that generalize across different data structures.
